definition: An extra security step after your password, e.g. a code via SMS or an app.
Computer programs that can learn and perform tasks independently, such as ChatGPT or Gemini.
The set of rules that, for example, YouTube or Facebook use to decide which videos or posts to show you, based on what you watched before.
The official value the municipality assigns to a property each year, used for things like property tax.
A file (photo, document) that you send along with an email.
An app (such as Google Authenticator) that generates a new, temporary login code for two-factor authentication — safer than a code via SMS.
A spare copy of your files or data, so you don't lose anything if your device breaks, gets lost, or is stolen.
When an AI program unintentionally gives unfair or skewed answers, because it was trained on data containing existing prejudices.
The program you use to view websites, such as Chrome, Edge or Safari.
A payment method (like Klarna) where you receive the product first and pay later — watch the payment deadline, or fees can quickly follow.
A scam where a criminal poses as your manager and, under time pressure, asks you to quickly transfer money or buy gift cards.
Storing files over the internet, instead of only on your own device.
A business's registration number with the Dutch Chamber of Commerce — a sign that a web shop genuinely exists.
Small files a website stores on your device, for example to remember that you're logged in, or to track your browsing behavior.
When a company's data (such as email addresses or passwords) is accidentally exposed or stolen through a hack.
An AI-generated, fake video or audio recording of a real person that looks genuine but isn't.
Your personal login method for the Dutch government, such as the Tax Office.
Information that is deliberately false or misleading, often spread to influence people.
The part of an internet address after the '@' (in email) or after 'www.' (on a website), for example 'ing.nl'. Always pay close attention to this when checking for phishing.
Retrieving a file from the internet and saving it to your own device.
A label (A through G) showing how energy-efficient a home is — important when buying or renting a house.
Checking whether a claim or news story is accurate, often done by specialized websites.
The effect where an algorithm mainly shows you opinions that match what you already think, so you see less of other viewpoints.
A phone setting that lets you decide which notifications come through, and which don't, at certain times.
When someone else uses your personal information to pretend to be you, for example to buy things in your name.
A browser window that doesn't remember browsing history or cookies after it's closed.
A scam where you're lured into 'investing' in crypto, stocks, or something else, often via a fake ad featuring a celebrity.
Checking a source by opening a new tab and searching what others say about it, instead of only judging the source itself.
A situation where you own a house but not the land underneath it — you pay an annual fee to the landowner instead.
Your right that a product must do what you can reasonably expect, separate from any warranty a shop offers itself.
Your personal digital mailbox at MijnOverheid, where official letters from the government arrive.
A pop-up message from an app or website, for example to let you know something new has happened.
A modern, more secure way to log in using your fingerprint or face, without a password.
A program that securely remembers all your passwords for you.
Fake messages that try to steal your password or data by pretending to be a trustworthy sender.
The question or instruction you type to an AI program such as ChatGPT.
The legal period (usually 14 days) during which you may return an online purchase, no reason needed.
Fake or bought reviews that make a product or web shop look better than it is.
Uploading a photo to a search engine to see where and when it has already appeared online before.
A scam where someone you got to know online (for example via a dating app) eventually asks you for money.
The PIN, pattern, or fingerprint that secures your phone or computer as soon as the screen turns off.
The email address a message comes from. In phishing this often looks real at first glance, but doesn't quite match up on closer inspection.
A trick where a criminal takes over your phone number, so SMS codes for 2FA get sent to them instead of you.
Manipulating people into giving up confidential information, often through pressure, urgency, or impersonated authority (like 'the bank' or 'your boss').
Unwanted or promotional email, which usually ends up automatically in a separate 'Spam' or 'Junk' folder.
Phishing aimed specifically at you personally, for example using your real name, based on information found about you.
Playing video or music directly over the internet (like Netflix or Spotify), without downloading the file first.
A 'free trial' that automatically turns into a paid subscription if you don't cancel in time.
An extra 'page' at the top of your browser that lets you have multiple websites open at once.
A Dutch trust mark for reliable web shops.
A link or code that lets you follow where your ordered parcel currently is.
An improved version of software, which often also closes security gaps — install these as soon as possible.
A program (like Siri or Google Assistant) that listens to your voice and carries out a command for you.
A small, instantly visible piece of an app on your home screen, such as the weather or your calendar.
